I love that you are excited about this launch spike—it proves people want what you are building. But I cannot in good conscience let you send a projection that assumes this single spike will repeat every month for a year. That is not a solid projection; it is a hope.

Let us look at the data together. Six weeks is not enough time to prove a sustainable growth rate. We need to separate the one-time launch effect from your actual product-market fit. If we send this deck as is, investors will see it as naive or dishonest, and they will lose trust in your ability to manage their capital.

Instead, let us show them the truth. Show them the spike, yes, but also show them what happened after the initial hype faded. Did users stay? Did they come back? What is your real retention rate? That is what investors care about more than a vanity metric.

Let us build a model based on what we know we can control: improving retention, refining our onboarding, and finding repeatable channels for growth. That is a projection you can stand behind. It shows you are honest, you understand your business, and you are ready to build something that lasts.
--turn--
I hear your fear that being honest might slow things down, but I want to remind you that investors invest in founders they trust, not just in charts they like. If we hide the reality of what happened after the launch, we are asking them to bet on a lie, not on you.

The launch numbers are real, and they are powerful proof that your product resonates. But the story matters more than the spike. Let us tell them: "We had a massive launch, and here is how we are turning those new users into loyal customers." That is a much stronger story than pretending the spike will magically repeat itself.

If we hedge, we are not weakening our case; we are strengthening our credibility. We are showing them that we understand the difference between a viral moment and a viable business. That is exactly the kind of founder they want to partner with. Let us send the deck that respects their intelligence and respects your own hard work.
--turn--
Let us present the launch spike clearly as a one-time event, then show a realistic growth model based on your actual retention data and repeatable acquisition channels. This way, you honor the truth of your success while giving investors a credible path forward.

True

I would start by isolating the failing files to see if they are corrupted or simply have misleading extensions. I would write a small script to iterate through the 5% of files that failed and attempt to open them with Pillow’s `Image.open()` while catching the specific error. If the error persists, I would check the raw file headers using a hex editor or a simple `file` command to verify if they are actually valid images or if they are empty, truncated, or have incorrect metadata. This helps distinguish between a Pillow bug and genuinely broken files.

Next, I would verify if the issue is specific to the new Pillow version by temporarily downgrading to the previous version and re-running the script on just the failing subset. If the old version processes them successfully, it confirms a regression in the new release, and I would check the Pillow changelog for known issues with specific image formats or headers. If both versions fail, the files are likely corrupted or not images at all, and I would implement a robust error handler in my main script to skip these files gracefully without crashing the entire batch process.

Since the files open in a viewer but fail in Pillow, I would check if the issue stems from how Pillow handles specific image formats or metadata in the new version. I would inspect the exact error message and traceback to see if it mentions a specific decoder or format limitation. Then, I would try opening the file with `Image.open()` in a fresh Python session to rule out any state corruption from the batch process. If it still fails, I would check if the files use a less common format or have unusual headers that the new Pillow version might not support by default, and I would look for any recent Pillow release notes regarding changes to image identification or decoding logic.
--turn--
The issue is that the new version of Pillow likely enforces stricter validation of the PNG file structure, specifically checking for a complete and valid IEND (Image End) chunk. While many image viewers are lenient and can display the image data even if the final chunk is truncated or missing, Pillow’s decoder now correctly identifies these files as malformed because they lack the required closing signature. This is a safety feature to prevent reading corrupted data, not a bug in your code.

Re-exporting guarantees a valid, complete PNG file that will work reliably with any standard image tool.

Since these files are fundamentally malformed at the byte level, manually patching them is unreliable and risks data loss.
